title: Tenant network pattern catalog and cutover checklist (draft)
summary: Working draft: compact catalog of tenant VPC reference patterns, recommended Terraform module guardrails, and a pragmatic cutover checklist for migrating tenant workloads from staging to customer VPCs (includes rollout and rollback guidance).
content:
Purpose:
This is an internal working draft that captures a concise set of verified tenant VPC topologies we use when onboarding customers to Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem). The goal is to have a small, opinionated catalog that engineers and Solutions Eng can use as starting points, plus a cutover checklist for staging->prod migrations and notes for Terraform modules and upgrades.

Scope:
- Multi-cloud patterns (AWS, GCP, Azure) but focused on the common primitives: tenant isolation, egress control, private model endpoints, and outbound data exfil protections.
- Terraform module guidance targeted to the tenant-provisioner modules we maintain in infra-modules.
- Migration/cutover steps for non-disruptive handoff during onboarding.

Quick guidance (TL;DR):
- Pick one of the patterns below based on customer constraints (network policy, regulatory, connectivity).
- Use the infra-modules/tenant-vpc module pinned to a patch (see "module notes").
- Always run the preflight validation (connectivity tests + routing sanity + certificate checks) before cutover window.
- If upgrading modules, prefer blue/green IAM & route table changes where possible to avoid broad network churn.

Pattern Catalog (names are intentionally short):
1) Isolated Tenant VPC (single-tenant, dedicated subnets)
   - Description: Each tenant gets a dedicated VPC (or VNet) with isolated private subnets for model serving and a separate management subnet for monitoring/proxies.
   - Use when: High compliance requirements, customer-managed NACLs, or on-prem cross-connects.
   - Key primitives: dedicated NAT or egress-only gateway, private endpoints (AWS: Interface endpoints for S3/SecretsManager; GCP: Private Service Connect), explicit route tables, Terraform state per-tenant.
   - Pros/Cons: Maximum isolation; higher cost and operational overhead.

2) Shared-host VPC with Tenant Segmentation (shared infra VPC + tenant overlay)
   - Description: Centralized VPC hosts shared infra (load balancers, model caches). Tenants occupy isolated subnets + security groups or logical segments.
   - Use when: Many small tenants, cost efficiency needed, less stringent network separation.
   - Key primitives: shared service endpoints, strict security group naming conventions, VNets/subnets tagged with tenant-id, central egress chokepoints.

3) Service-per-tenant overlay (Hub-and-Spoke with Transit gateway)
   - Description: Hub (central infra) + spokes for each tenant. Hub runs shared routers (transit gateway, cloud-router) that mediate connectivity and central observability.
   - Use when: Need central routing policies, simplified cross-tenant peering controls, or when connecting many spoke networks (customer on-prem to hub).
   - Notes: Use explicit route propagation policies and prefix lists for service IPs.

4) Air-gapped / On-prem Appliance pattern
   - Description: Customer provides isolated on-prem network with a dedicated appliance or VM cluster. Redwood packages can be deployed in this network; control-plane traffic flows via a dedicated, customer-approved tunnel.
   - Use when: Regulated data that cannot egress public cloud, or for low-latency local inference.
   - Key actions: PKI provisioning, offline package signing, KMS/HSM integration notes.

Pattern Decision Matrix (short):
- Compliance / High-Reg: Isolated Tenant VPC or Air-gapped
- Cost-Constrain & Many Tenants: Shared-host VPC
- Complex On-prem Connectivity: Hub-and-Spoke

Terraform module notes (practical guardrails):
- Module composition: Keep modules small and composable: tenant-network (VPC/VNet + subnets), tenant-network-attachments (Peering / Transit associations), tenant-network-nat (NAT/gateway + egress policies).
- Inputs we always require: tenant_id, env (staging|prod), allowed_cidrs (list), admin_contact (email), deploy_region, dns_zone_id.
- Outputs we use in other modules: vpc_id, subnet_ids (comma-delimited if cross-language), route_table_ids, peering_connection_ids.
- State backend: Use per-tenant state file in remote backend (S3/GCS + DynamoDB/GCS locking) to limit blast radius. Name pattern: redwood-tenant-<tenant_id>-<env>-tfstate.
- Versioning: Pin major and minor versions in customer-specific terraform manifests. Only bump module major version in controlled upgrade windows.

Sample recommended snippet (pseudo-tf for composition):
  module "tenant_vpc" {
    source = "github.com/redwood-inference/infra-modules//tenant-network?ref=v0.14.3"
    tenant_id = var.tenant_id
    env = var.env
    allowed_cidrs = var.allowed_cidrs
  }

Preflight validations (automated checks to run pre-cutover):
- IP plan validation: Ensure no overlapping CIDRs with customer on-prem or other tenant VPCs.
- Route validation: Verify route tables have expected targets (nat vs igw) and no broad 0.0.0.0/0 to unexpected attachments.
- DNS validation: Ensure private zones are created and resolvable from tenant subnets.
- Endpoint reachability: curl/tcp checks to model endpoints, metrics endpoints, and KMS/secret endpoints.
- Certificate check: Confirm certs for private endpoints are present and chain validates.
- Billing/quotas: Quick check for quota limits (ENIs, IP addresses) in the chosen region.

Cutover checklist (staging -> customer VPC):
Pre-cutover (72–48 hrs):
- Confirm signed agreement & network contact.
- Finalize tenant CIDR allocations and announce to infra-ops. Create a change record (INF-CHANGE-XXXX).
- Ensure Terraform module version is pinned in the customer manifest and PR created (link to PR in linked_artifacts).
- Run an infrastructure plan in a sandbox tenant account and capture plan output.
- Run preflight validations and record results.
- Schedule cutover window with the customer and notify oncall (infra-oncall slack & email: infra-ops@redwood.com).

Cutover Day (window):
- Step 1: Apply infra changes to provision networking (terraform apply). Use remote state locking and small apply batches (subnets -> routing -> endpoints).
- Step 2: Validate control-plane connectivity to private endpoints (3 consecutive checks, 1 minute apart).
- Step 3: Deploy model-serving pods and sidecar (if applicable) to staging subnets; do not flip traffic yet.
- Step 4: Swap DNS records / update LB to point to new target groups (or update route table for internal switch).
- Step 5: Gradually route 10% -> 50% -> 100% traffic using canary steps or weight-based routing. Monitor latency, error rates, and CPU/GPU utilization.
- Step 6: Run smoke tests and customer acceptance tests.

Rollback steps (if anything fails):
- Revert DNS / LB weights to previous target (immediate).
- If terraform apply introduced a faulty route, revert terraform (apply previous plan file) or remove problematic attachment.
- If state is inconsistent, lock further apply and escalate to infra-ops for manual reconciliation.

Upgrade plan for modules (safe path):
- Stage 1: Create a compatibility matrix for the current infra and desired module changes. Identify any breaking changes (resource renames, lifecycle meta-args).
- Stage 2: Run a dry-run plan in a sandbox tenant using the new module ref; compare created/destroyed count.
- Stage 3: For non-disruptive changes (tags, description), roll out via small batch using CI.
- Stage 4: For disruptive changes (resource recreation), prepare blue/green pattern (create new subnets/resources, switch routes), migrate live sessions if required, then destroy old resources.
- Pre-approve by SRE and Security before prod module rollouts.

Operational notes and gotchas (learning from recent onboards):
- ENI and private IP exhaustion: Prefer subnets with /24 or larger where service scale is high. Document expected IP consumption per GPU host.
- Cloud provider semantics: GCP private service connect has different DNS/MTU behavior vs AWS interface endpoints — run MTU checks for large model payloads.
- Terraform import: When a customer already created some resources, import them into per-tenant state with documented import plan. Test import in a sandbox first.
- Drift detection: Schedule periodic terraform plan runs and alert on unexpected diffs for route tables and NACLs.

Security & compliance notes:
- KMS/HSM: For air-gapped or regulated tenants, integrate with customer KMS and keep keys in customer project/tenant. Document key rotation process.
- Audit logs: Ensure flow logs (VPC flow logs) are enabled and streamed to the customer's logging endpoint; verify retention policy.
- Least-privilege: IAM roles the tenant-provisioner uses must be scoped to the tenant state and resource naming prefixes. Avoid cross-tenant roles.

Open questions / action items (owners):
- Q1: Standardize naming convention for peering connections across clouds (owner: Diego)
- Q2: Add an automated CIDR overlap detector to onboarding pipeline (owner: Ruth)
- Q3: Validate MTU behavior for GCP PSC with model payload sizes > 64KB (owner: Kofi)
- Q4: Draft customer-facing one-pager summarizing expected downtime windows for different patterns (owner: Asha)

Appendix: sample sanity checks and commands (examples)
- Basic route table sanity (AWS): aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC_ID}
- TLS check to private endpoint (Linux): echo | openssl s_client -connect private-model.example.internal:443 -servername private-model.example.internal
- Terraform plan with target (if you must apply incrementally): terraform plan -target=module.tenant_vpc.module.subnets -out=plan.subnets.tfplan

Notes to self: this doc is intentionally terse and tactical — convert into a longer onboarding playbook and customer checklist once owners close open questions. Expect this to be iterated in the onboarding runbook repo and linked to the tenant-provisioner PR for module changes.
